item.title: Screwworm Detected for First Time in Arizona as Outbreak Spreads
item.description: New World screwworm was found in Arizona for the first time, detected in a dog, as cases of the deadly parasite accelerate.
item.dc:creator: list.metadata.agency
item.content:encoded: (Bloomberg) -- New World screwworm was found in Arizona for the first time, detected in a dog, as cases of the deadly parasite accelerate.The US Department of Agriculture confirmed the infection late Wednesday in a dog in Cochise County, Arizona. The spread of the parasitic fly, whose larvae burrow into the wounds of animals, had remained relatively contained since the pest was first detected in the US in June. Most of the early cases were limited to Texas. However, the pace of infections has increased this month, particularly in New Mexico. There have been a total of 71 cases of screwworm in the US since the outbreak began, according to the USDA. Eighteen are still active, with 10 located in New Mexico. The increase in October comes after screwworm, which can be deadly to livestock if left untreated, was discovered for the first time in wildlife last week. Spread among wildlife has been a key concern for cattle ranchers since the animals travel through the same terrain that their herds graze on. The spread also comes as the USDA has reopened ports in Arizona and New Mexico to shipments of cattle from Mexico. The US had halted livestock shipments from the country, and largely maintained that ban until late August when it began a phased reopening of the ports. The US had previously eradicated screwworm, pushing the pest south of Panama. But the fly began spreading north again after the pandemic, reaching Mexico in late 2024. While screwworm is a major threat to the US cattle herd, the parasite has also infected animals from goats to horses. The most recent five cases involved four dogs and one cat.More stories like this are available on bloomberg.com©2026 Bloomberg L.P.

item.title: Alvin Hellerstein, Judge in Maduro, 9/11 Cases, Dies at 92
item.description: Veteran federal judge Alvin Hellerstein, who oversaw cases against Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, Archegos Capital Management family office founder Bill Hwang and litigation over the 9/11 terrorist attack, died at 92.
item.dc:creator: list.metadata.agency
item.content:encoded: (Bloomberg) -- Veteran federal judge Alvin Hellerstein, who oversaw cases against Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, Archegos Capital Management family office founder Bill Hwang and litigation over the 9/11 terrorist attack, died at 92. The Jewish Center, a synagogue in Manhattan, notified congregants that Hellerstein, a longtime member and trustee, had died. The US District Court for the Southern District of New York said the the judge passed away Wednesday morning, surrounded by family.“Judge Hellerstein was an insightful and dedicated lawyer who, following a distinguished career in the private sector, served with distinction for over 25 years as a distinguished jurist of this court,” Chief Judge Laura Swain said in a statement. “His energetic and dedicated service to this court continued until his death.”Hellerstein, a native New Yorker, served in the Army’s Judge Advocate General’s Corps before joining New York City law firm Stroock & Stroock & Lavan LLP in 1960. He was appointed to the bench by President Bill Clinton in 1998. Since then, he has overseen high-profile white collar prosecutions and complex litigation. Most recently, he was overseeing the narco-terrorism case against Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores. The couple are scheduled to face trial in June. New judges will be assigned at random to the Maduro case and the other cases Hellerstein was overseeing.During his early years on the bench, Hellerstein built his reputation overseeing yearslong litigation related to the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks. In 2010, he rejected a settlement for 10,000 rescue and cleanup workers who fell ill working at Ground Zero because the payouts may have been too small after attorney fees were taken out. Months later, Hellerstein approved a $712 million pact well over the original proposal. In a separate case, he ruled against families seeking to recover human remains from the 9/11 debris. In the courtroom, the Columbia Law School graduate was famous for interrupting lawyers who weren’t questioning witnesses to his satisfaction or losing the jury’s attention. In the 2024 criminal trial of Hwang, whose family office meltdown caused chaos across Wall Street, Hellerstein interrupted the questioning of a witness to announce the birth of his great-grandchild. “It’s a gorgeous baby,” remarked Hellerstein as he turned his phone to bemused lawyers in the courtroom. The jury erupted in applause. In the same trial, he chided a lawyer for boring the jury to tears. ‘Just and Measured’He sentenced Hwang to 18 years in prison, a decision that the judge never took lightly.In rare public comments, Hellerstein, an Orthodox Jew, has spoken about how his faith intersected with his work. He told a podcast in 2020 that he held sentencing hearings on Fridays so he could used Sabbath to reflect on the consequences of his decisions.“I never ever have had the feeling that my punishment was just and measured,” he said. “And that’s good. I think a judge should be disconcerted with what he does. I’m taking away the liberty of someone.” In recent years, Hellerstein oversaw trials involving Charlie Javice, the start-up founder convicted of defrauding JPMorgan Chase, as well as a human rights case against BNP Paribas. Roger Stavis, the head of Mintz & Gold’s white collar defense practice, who’s tried cases before Hellerstein, recalled him having a sense of humor that made him likeable even when Stavis was losing. ‘Dayenu’In one hearing in Hellerstein’s courtroom in lower Manhattan, Stavis recalled objecting to the prosecution introducing the same evidence over and over. The judge shot back at Stavis, asking him to identify the legal precedent on how many times is too many. “I said ‘United States v. Dayenu’ — the Hebrew term for it would have been enough — and he started cracking up,” Stavis said. item.title: US goods trade deficit widens in September as AI boom drives imports to record high
item.description: According to Reuters, US goods trade deficit widened from $2.8 billion to $134.9 billion in September. While imports of goods increase $8.1 billion to $344.1 billion, goods exports climbed from $5.3 billion to $209.2 billion.
item.dc:creator: Sneha Biswas
item.content:encoded: The US trade deficit in goods widened more than expected in September. This comes as imports climbed to a record high. According to Reuters, the surge is driven by demand for capital goods associated with the artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure boom, indicating that trade could have weighed heavily on economic growth in the third quarter. The latest deterioration in the trade balance is reported by the Commerce Department on Wednesday, as per the news agency. Reportedly, it prompted some economists to estimate that trade may have shaved as much as four percentage points off Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth in the July-September quarter. However, the government's advance estimate of third-quarter GDP, scheduled for release on Thursday, is still expected to show strong growth, supported by a surge in AI-related investments and resilient consumer spending. "Although trade will weigh on quarterly GDP, this is a sign of strength rather than weakness for the US economy as it signifies continued business investment and momentum for consumer spending," said Daniel Vielhaber, an economist at Nationwide, as quoted by Reuters. US goods trade The goods trade deficit rose 2.1%, or $2.8 billion, to $134.9 billion in September. It marked the highest level since March 2025, the Commerce Department's Census Bureau said. Economists surveyed by Reuters had predicted the deficit to come in at $130.2 billion. The goods trade gap continued to widen through the third quarter. Imports of goods increased 2.4%, or $8.1 billion, to a record $344.1 billion in September, led by a 7.5% increase in capital goods. Capital goods imports surged 77.2% from a year earlier. "So much of the hardware that the tech companies need is coming from overseas, driving a massive widening in the trade gap," said Stephen Stanley, chief US economist at Santander US Capital Markets to Reuters. Imports vs exports Besides the AI investment boom, sustained consumer spending despite rising living costs has also been cited as contributing to the increase in imports. Consumer goods imports rose 3.1% in September, while imports of other goods increased 6.7%. Imports of industrial supplies, which include gold and petroleum, declined 6.0%. For the unversed, gold is excluded from the calculation of GDP. Imports of food and motor vehicles also fell during the month. In terms of export, shipments of goods increased $5.3 billion, or 2.6%, to $209.2 billion in September. Food exports jumped 12.8%, while exports of capital goods rose 5.4% and consumer products advanced 6.5%. Exports of motor vehicles and industrial supplies also saw a decline, Reuters reported. Trade weighs on GDP growth Economists estimated that trade could subtract four percentage points from GDP growth in the third quarter, while those at Oxford Economics put the drag at 3.25 percentage points. Trade has not contributed to US GDP growth for three consecutive quarters, added the report. However, it is believed that a portion of September's imports ended up as unsold inventory at wholesalers and retailers, which could potentially help cushion the impact on GDP. The Census Bureau reported that wholesale inventories increased 0.6% in September. Reportedly, retail inventories rose 0.3%. Stocks at motor vehicle and parts dealers increased 0.2%. Apart from motor vehicles and parts, retail inventories rose 0.4% in September after edging up 0.1% in August. Previously, a Reuters survey of economists had forecast the US economy to grow at an annualised rate of 3.2% in the third quarter, compared with 2.2% in the second quarter.
